idiom_name: abstract/open class with protected primitives and protected abstract activate() (AbstractMutableList shape)
implementation_notes: Kotlin's declarations are final by default, so the intent is spelled out: the base is abstract (or open), the primitives are protected, and the sandbox method is protected abstract with override on the subclass side. The standard library uses exactly this shape in kotlin.collections.AbstractMutableList, whose protected modCount and protected helper members exist for subclasses such as ArrayList while the list algorithms stay in the base; the visibility-modifiers chapter defines protected as 'visible in this class and its subclasses' (not the package, unlike Java) and internal as module-wide, which is the closest thing Kotlin has to a sandbox shared with a module's tests. A sealed class freezes the family while keeping the shared primitive set. Where behaviours share no state, a value of engine functions passed to a function replaces the hierarchy; the class form is justified when the family shares stored state and an extension lifecycle.
pitfalls: An open primitive can be overridden by a subclass that then changes the vocabulary for its whole subtree; leave primitives non-open (the default) and keep only the sandbox method overridable.

Kotlin's protected is not package-visible but internal is module-visible: a primitive marked internal to share it with tests is also callable from every other class in the module, so the sandbox wall becomes a module wall.
The base class and its members must be marked open or abstract to be extensible at all - forgetting it turns an intended extension point into a compile error for the behaviour author.
A base-class constructor that calls the sandbox method runs before the subclass's property initialisers, so the behaviour reads uninitialised properties.
